query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor reactive additive to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that in situ forms a high‐temperature stable, self‐lubricating tribofilm during sliding will lower both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi HEA matrix with an initially coarse-grained, single-phase microstructure
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a small amount of a reactive additive that is designed to precipitate a lubricious, high-temperature stable phase at the sliding interface
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests executed from room temperature to 800 °C under variable normal loads and in both inert (e.g., ultra-high vacuum) and mildly oxidizing environments
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic formation of a nanoscale tribofilm combined with shear-induced grain refinement at the contact surface
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions the reactive additive enables the formation of an in situ lubricious phase that lowers the interfacial shear strength and, together with the activation of grain boundary sliding due to dynamic grain refinement (inverse Hall-Petch behavior), reduces friction and wear. This tribofilm continuously regenerates during sliding and adapts to temperature and load variations, maintaining low friction and wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified material will show a significantly and consistently lower friction coefficient and a reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy shows variable friction and wear performance, with increased friction and wear at higher temperatures due to mechanisms such as oxide layer fracturing and plastic deformation.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under sliding conditions typical of tribological testing (with applied loads and sliding speeds representative of practical applications) and in environments where no additional lubricants are provided.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal additive type, concentration, and phase kinetics of tribofilm formation remain to be determined; furthermore, the long-term stability and reproducibility of the tribofilm under cyclic loading and environmental variations are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi specimens and another set with a controlled minor addition of the reactive additive. Perform pin-on-disk sliding tests across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under varying normal loads in controlled inert and mildly oxidizing environments. After the tests, characterize the wear tracks using high-resolution microscopy and phase analysis (e.g., XRD, SEM) to detect the presence and morphology of any tribofilms.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of the sliding interface (including tribofilm thickness and integrity)
Phase identification of surface modifications post-sliding
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified CoCrFeNi samples do not consistently exhibit lower friction coefficients and lower wear rates than the baseline specimens across the full temperature range, or if a self-lubricating tribofilm is not reliably observed at the sliding interface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation. The microstructural characteristics of the AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings after the high temperature wear resistance test shows a highly favorable impact on microstructure stability and wear resistance, due to its the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetallic compounds.
